[2] Dr. Okafor: Most students reread their notes the night before an exam.
[3] Dr. Okafor: Rereading feels productive because the material looks familiar.
[4] Dr. Okafor: Familiarity is not the same as being able to recall it.
[5] Dr. Okafor: The first technique I want you to know is retrieval practice.
[6] Dr. Okafor: Retrieval practice means closing the book and trying to recall what you just studied.
[7] Dr. Okafor: Every successful recall strengthens the memory, and every failed attempt shows you exactly what to revisit.
[8] Priya: So is it like using flashcards?
[9] Dr. Okafor: Flashcards are one way, yes.
[10] Dr. Okafor: A blank sheet of paper works too.
[11] Dr. Okafor: Write down everything you remember about a topic, then check it against your notes.
[12] Dr. Okafor: The second technique is spaced practice.
[13] Dr. Okafor: Instead of one long session, you split your study into shorter sessions spread over days.
[14] Dr. Okafor: A simple schedule is to review on day one, again on day three, and again on day seven.
[15] Dr. Okafor: Spacing works because a little forgetting between sessions makes the next recall harder, and that effort is what builds durable memory.
[16] Dr. Okafor: Cramming skips that effort, so the knowledge fades quickly after the exam.
[17] Priya: Sorry, my connection dropped for a second.
[18] Priya: Can you repeat the schedule?
[19] Dr. Okafor: Of course.
[20] Dr. Okafor: Day one, day three, day seven.
[21] Dr. Okafor: Each review should start with recall, not with rereading.
[22] Dr. Okafor: Before we continue, a quick logistics note.
[23] Dr. Okafor: Assignment two is due on Friday, and the submission portal closes at midnight.
[24] Dr. Okafor: Late work loses marks automatically, so please do not wait until the last hour.
[25] Dr. Okafor: Okay, the third technique is interleaving.
[26] Dr. Okafor: Interleaving means mixing different kinds of problems within one session instead of practising one kind repeatedly.
[27] Dr. Okafor: Suppose you are learning three types of maths problems.
[28] Dr. Okafor: Blocked practice means doing ten of type A, then ten of type B.
[29] Dr. Okafor: Interleaved practice means shuffling A, B and C together.
[30] Dr. Okafor: It feels harder and slower, but it teaches you to choose the right method, not only to apply one you already know.
[31] Priya: Does that help with exams where you do not know which method to use?
[32] Dr. Okafor: Exactly.
[33] Dr. Okafor: In an exam nobody tells you which type of problem you are facing, so interleaving trains that decision.
[34] Dr. Okafor: The fourth technique is elaboration.
[35] Dr. Okafor: Elaboration means explaining an idea in your own words and connecting it to something you already know.
[36] Dr. Okafor: If you cannot explain it simply, you probably do not understand it yet.
[37] Dr. Okafor: A practical version is the explain-back method.
[38] Dr. Okafor: After studying, explain the topic aloud as if teaching a friend, and note where you get stuck.
[39] Dr. Okafor: To sum up, the four techniques are retrieval practice, spaced practice, interleaving and elaboration.
[40] Dr. Okafor: All four make studying feel harder in the moment, and that difficulty is useful because it forces your memory to work.
[41] Dr. Okafor: For next week, pick one technique and apply it to your own course material.
[42] Dr. Okafor: Bring one example of what you tried and what you noticed.
</source>

List the 6 most important ideas a student must remember. Each idea is one clear sentence in your own words.

Example of the format, on unrelated material about gardening ("Tomatoes need six hours of sun."):
{"items":[{"quote":"Tomatoes need six hours of sun","idea":"Tomato plants need plenty of direct sunlight each day."}]}

Now do the same for the SOURCE above.

items.quote: Retrieval practice means closing the book and trying to recall what you just studied.
items.idea: Retrieval practice involves testing yourself on material you have just studied without looking at your notes.

items.quote: Instead of one long session, you split your study into shorter sessions spread over days.
items.idea: Spaced practice suggests dividing your study time into several shorter sessions spread out over multiple days.

items.quote: A little forgetting between sessions makes the next recall harder, and that effort is what builds durable memory.
items.idea: The effort required to recall information after a short period of forgetting is what helps build strong, lasting memories.

items.quote: Interleaving means mixing different kinds of problems within one session instead of practising one kind repeatedly.
items.idea: Interleaving involves mixing various types of problems during a single study session rather than practicing just one type over and over.

items.quote: Elaboration means explaining an idea in your own words and connecting it to something you already know.
items.idea: Elaboration is the process of explaining a concept in your own language and linking it to existing knowledge.

items.quote: All four make studying feel harder in the moment, and that difficulty is useful because it forces your memory to work.
items.idea: These four study techniques might feel more difficult while you are studying, but this difficulty is beneficial because it actively engages your memory.

lines.line: To wrap up, all four of these techniques might make studying feel tougher right away, but that difficulty is actually helpful because it pushes your memory to engage.

<source>
[0] Dr. Okafor: Welcome back to Learning Strategies.
[1] Dr. Okafor: Today's session is about why some study habits work and others only feel like they work.
[2] Dr. Okafor: Most students reread their notes the night before an exam.
[3] Dr. Okafor: Rereading feels productive because the material looks familiar.
[4] Dr. Okafor: Familiarity is not the same as being able to recall it.
[5] Dr. Okafor: The first technique I want you to know is retrieval practice.
[6] Dr. Okafor: Retrieval practice means closing the book and trying to recall what you just studied.
[7] Dr. Okafor: Every successful recall strengthens the memory, and every failed attempt shows you exactly what to revisit.
[8] Priya: So is it like using flashcards?
[9] Dr. Okafor: Flashcards are one way, yes.
[10] Dr. Okafor: A blank sheet of paper works too.
[11] Dr. Okafor: Write down everything you remember about a topic, then check it against your notes.
[12] Dr. Okafor: The second technique is spaced practice.
[13] Dr. Okafor: Instead of one long session, you split your study into shorter sessions spread over days.
[14] Dr. Okafor: A simple schedule is to review on day one, again on day three, and again on day seven.
[15] Dr. Okafor: Spacing works because a little forgetting between sessions makes the next recall harder, and that effort is what builds durable memory.
[16] Dr. Okafor: Cramming skips that effort, so the knowledge fades quickly after the exam.
[17] Priya: Sorry, my connection dropped for a second.
[18] Priya: Can you repeat the schedule?
[19] Dr. Okafor: Of course.
[20] Dr. Okafor: Day one, day three, day seven.
[21] Dr. Okafor: Each review should start with recall, not with rereading.
[22] Dr. Okafor: Before we continue, a quick logistics note.
[23] Dr. Okafor: Assignment two is due on Friday, and the submission portal closes at midnight.
[24] Dr. Okafor: Late work loses marks automatically, so please do not wait until the last hour.
[25] Dr. Okafor: Okay, the third technique is interleaving.
[26] Dr. Okafor: Interleaving means mixing different kinds of problems within one session instead of practising one kind repeatedly.
[27] Dr. Okafor: Suppose you are learning three types of maths problems.
[28] Dr. Okafor: Blocked practice means doing ten of type A, then ten of type B.
[29] Dr. Okafor: Interleaved practice means shuffling A, B and C together.
[30] Dr. Okafor: It feels harder and slower, but it teaches you to choose the right method, not only to apply one you already know.
[31] Priya: Does that help with exams where you do not know which method to use?
[32] Dr. Okafor: Exactly.
[33] Dr. Okafor: In an exam nobody tells you which type of problem you are facing, so interleaving trains that decision.
[34] Dr. Okafor: The fourth technique is elaboration.
[35] Dr. Okafor: Elaboration means explaining an idea in your own words and connecting it to something you already know.
[36] Dr. Okafor: If you cannot explain it simply, you probably do not understand it yet.
[37] Dr. Okafor: A practical version is the explain-back method.
[38] Dr. Okafor: After studying, explain the topic aloud as if teaching a friend, and note where you get stuck.
[39] Dr. Okafor: To sum up, the four techniques are retrieval practice, spaced practice, interleaving and elaboration.
[40] Dr. Okafor: All four make studying feel harder in the moment, and that difficulty is useful because it forces your memory to work.
[41] Dr. Okafor: For next week, pick one technique and apply it to your own course material.
[42] Dr. Okafor: Bring one example of what you tried and what you noticed.
</source>

Suggest 3 short project prompts a student could do to show what they learned (for example make a poster, record a 2-minute talk, or apply the idea to their own situation). Each has a "title" and a 1-2 sentence "brief". The quote is the passage the project is about.

Example of the format, on unrelated material about gardening ("Tomatoes need six hours of sun."):
{"items":[{"quote":"Tomatoes need six hours of sun","title":"Sun map","brief":"Sketch your garden and mark where each spot gets direct light, then decide where a tomato plant would go."}]}

Now do the same for the SOURCE above.

items.quote: Retrieval practice means closing the book and trying to recall what you just studied.
items.title: Recall Challenge Log
items.brief: Choose a topic from your course material and practice retrieval by closing your notes and writing down everything you remember. Note how difficult or easy the recall felt.

items.quote: Instead of one long session, you split your study into shorter sessions spread over days.
items.title: Spaced Study Plan
items.brief: Design a study schedule for a difficult topic, ensuring you split the material into shorter sessions spread out over several days, following a pattern like day one, day three, and day seven.

items.quote: Interleaving means mixing different kinds of problems within one session instead of practising one kind repeatedly.
items.title: Mixed Practice Set
items.brief: If you are studying different types of problems, create a practice set that mixes them up rather than doing all of one type consecutively. Reflect on how this mixing feels compared to blocked practice.

items.quote: Elaboration means explaining an idea in your own words and connecting it to something you already know.
items.title: Explain-Back Demonstration
items.brief: Select a complex idea from your course and record yourself explaining it aloud as if you were teaching a friend. Identify specific points where you struggled to explain it simply.
